title: Resolve default accent color for Meridian extension

messages.content: We need a better logo for meridian. A minimal, flat style
messages.editable_content: We need a better logo for meridian. A minimal, flat style
messages.delivery_content: We need a better logo for meridian. A minimal, flat style

messages.content: I'll look at what Meridian has now before proposing anything. Good — I have the current mark, the palette, and rendering tools. Let me diagnose and then build candidates. Clear results. The current mark collapses to a smear below 32px — confirming the diagnosis. Let me tune the three that survived. Two clear winners. Let me stress-test them where it actually matters — the browser toolbar, light and dark, plus the brand accent. Locked. Writing the assets to a proposal folder — I'm not overwriting your live `img/` files without your say-so. Open **`img/logo-proposal/preview.html`** to see it in context. ## What's wrong with the current mark I rendered it down the size ramp first, and the problem is structural, not aesthetic: 1. **It dies below 32px.** The M is a calligraphic brush form built from three tapered strokes separated by hairline gaps. Those gaps are ~2px at 124 units — at 16px they close completely and the mark becomes a dark smear inside a ring. Your toolbar icon and favicon are *only* ever seen at 16–32px, so the logo fails at the only sizes that matter. 2. **Two unrelated design systems in one lockup.** An organic, high-contrast script letterform sitting inside a rigid geometric ring. They share no stroke weight, no terminal style, no grid — so they read as a sticker on a circle rather than one object. 3. **Extreme stroke contrast.** The ring is a constant 8u; the M swells from ~14u to under 2u. Uneven weight is exactly what makes a mark shimmer and break up when rasterized small. 4. **It forced a hack.** `icon-source.svg` has to paint an opaque `#f5f5f7` plate behind the mark just to stay visible on dark Chrome toolbars — a symptom of a mark that can't carry itself. ## The proposal **A geometric M knocked out of a solid disc.** - **Solid mass beats strokes at small sizes.** The disc is unbroken ink, so the silhouette is stable at any resolution; the M reads as negative space, which stays open where thin positive strokes would fill in. It's crisp at 16px in all three color roles — I verified rasterized, not just by eye at 128. - **One vocabulary.** Single 13u stroke weight, round caps and joins throughout, built on a 128 grid with the disc at r=52 (12u of clear space). Nothing tapers, nothing competes. - **You keep the M.** This is an evolution, not a rebrand — the monogram equity carries over, it just gets a form that survives. - **Optical correction applied:** round caps push the M's visual mass 2u below true center, so the letterform is drawn 2u high. It's mathematically off-center and looks centered — which is the one that counts. I also tested a globe/meridian-arc route. It rendered beautifully but I rejected it: a circle-with-meridian is the universal "web/language/internet" icon, and on a *browser extension* it reads as generic chrome rather than as your brand. **The teal disc (`#0ABAFF`) clears both light and dark toolbars from a single asset** — so you can delete the white-plate workaround in `icon-source.svg` entirely. ## Files In `img/logo-proposal/` — nothing live was touched: - `meridian-mark.svg` — master, fills with `currentColor` so it inherits `--text-primary` anywhere in the UI - `favicon.svg` — theme-aware via `prefers-color-scheme`, matching your existing pattern - `icon-source.svg` + `icon16/32/48/128.png` — toolbar set in brand teal - `meridian-mark-l.svg` / `-d.svg` — flat-color variants for `` contexts Two things worth deciding before I wire it in: whether you want the toolbar icon in **teal** (distinctive, one asset, but fixed against your auto-derived accent) or **monochrome theme-aware** (quieter, matches the current behavior). And say the word if you want me to swap the live `img/` assets and update `manifest.json` — plus check `utils/toolbarIcon.js` and `utils/favicon.js`, which have tests referencing the current geometry.

# 3a: meridian slot, off-center (a meridian, not a bisector)
cat > d3.svg <<'EOF'

<path fill="#1c1c1e" fill-rule="evenodd" d="M64 12a52 52 0 1 1 0 104 52 52 0 0 1 0-104Z M44 15h11v98h-11Z"/>

# 5: M whose apexes touch the ring — one integrated system, no floating monogram
cat > d5.svg <<'EOF'

<g fill="none" stroke="#1c1c1e" stroke-width="12" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round">

<mask id="m"><rect width="128" height="128" fill="#fff"/>

<circle cx="64" cy="64" r="52" fill="#1c1c1e" mask="url(#m)"/>

for f in d1 d2 d3 d4 d5 d6; do
  for s in 128 48 32 16; do inkscape "$f.svg" -w $s -h $s -o "${f}_${s}.png" 2>/dev/null; done
  magick -background '#f5f5f5' -alpha remove -alpha off "${f}_128.png" "${f}_48.png" "${f}_32.png" "${f}_16.png" \
    -bordercolor '#f5f5f5' -border 14 -gravity center +append "row_$f.png"
done
magick row_d1.png row_d2.png row_d3.png row_d4.png row_d5.png row_d6.png -background '#f5f5f5' -gravity west -append sheet2.png
echo done",

Good instinct — and it's worth being precise about *why* it works, because that determines how far to take it.

Let me look at the actual tab switcher before I propose anything for it.

`WorkspaceLane` — you already have "lanes." That's a route line waiting to happen. Let me read it.

Now I can see the real opportunity. Let me check how tab cards lay out inside a lane.

It's an auto-fill **grid**, not a single row — so a horizontal rail would only work on one line of cards. That changes the answer. Let me build the demo.

Open **`img/logo-proposal/metro.html`**. The instinct holds up — and there's a better reason for it than vibe.

## The concept closes on itself

A transit roundel is **a line crossing a circle**. That is literally what a meridian *is*. So the metro device isn't borrowed styling — it's a diagram of the product's name. That's the rare case where a visual language and a brand name are the same idea, and it's worth building on.

It also means the mark can stop being a logo and start being a **system**: the logo is a stop on the Meridian line, and the tab switcher uses that same line. One vocabulary, top to bottom.

## Three lockups, different jobs

- **A · Station stop** — mark on the rail, `MERIDIAN` letterspaced. This is the system-defining one.
- **B · Nameplate** — platform signage. Splash, store hero, README banner only. Honest flag: circle + bar + name sits close to the TfL roundel, so I kept ours a solid disc with the mark riding *on* the plate rather than inside a ring. Different enough, but you should know the neighborhood.
- **C · Quiet lockup** — what actually belongs in your top bar. Not everything should shout.

Your `.lane-title` is already uppercase at `0.05em` tracking — that's transit signage type. The wordmark just matches what you'd already built.

## The tab switcher part — I had to change your idea

I checked before drawing. `.tab-grid` is `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(180px, 1fr))` — a **wrapping grid**, not a row. A horizontal route line only works on a single row; on row two it vanishes. So the literal subway-map reading fails on your actual layout.

What works instead is a **vertical spine**: the line descends from the lane's station marker down the full height of the lane, terminating in a rounded cap. Wrapping-agnostic, works at any tab count.

And it earns its place functionally. Your lane color exists today as a **10px dot** — a single point, easy to miss, gone from awareness the moment you scroll into a long lane. Promoting it to a line converts a point into a continuously trackable channel. Gestalt's *uniform connectedness* groups more strongly than proximity or similarity — which is exactly the claim a lane is trying to make. The color also stays **redundant** with the lane title, so it never becomes sole-encoding for colorblind users.

I also changed the dot to a **ring**, so the spine has something to visibly terminate into — it reads as a station, not a stray bullet.

## What I'd leave out

- **No 45° diagonals or route topology.** A subway map is optimized for a fixed, known network. Your tab set is arbitrary and reflows constantly — diagonals would break on every resize and carry zero information.
- **No line-name badges or "interchange" markers.** Pure costume, real clutter.
- **Spine stays at 55% opacity until lane hover.** Your wallpaper is user-set; saturated chrome would fight it.

One integration note: the spine CSS assumes a `.lane-body` wrapper around `.tab-grid`, which `WorkspaceLane.js` doesn't currently render. It can also hang off `.workspace-lane::before` with a hardcoded top offset for the header — but that's a magic number that'll drift. I'd add the wrapper.

Want me to build the spine into `meridian.css` and `WorkspaceLane.js` for real, or keep iterating on the lockups first?

messages.content:
Good question — and the answer depends on a measurement, so let me characterize the mark's M precisely first.

Thin local selection. Let me try pulling the real candidates.

No network in this sandbox. Let me work with what's installed and derive the spec from the geometry instead.

The overlay is the useful part — blue is the mark's M, grey is each typeface. Look at what it exposes.

## What I measured

The mark's M has a specific, unusual set of traits:

| Trait | Value |
|---|---|
| Stroke | Monolinear, 13/128 — zero contrast |
| Terminals | Fully round (radius = ½ stroke) |
| Proportion | 53 × 53 — **exactly square** |
| Stems | Perfectly vertical, zero splay |
| Vertex | Descends **60%** — stops well short of the baseline |
| Substrate | Perfect circle |

## The finding

**Every text typeface I tested has a vertex that runs all the way to the baseline, and all of them are narrower than square.** You can see it in the overlay — the blue vertex floats above the grey one, every row.

That's not a coincidence and it's not a gap in the sample. A text face *needs* a full-depth vertex, because at 12px a shortened one closes into a blob. I shortened yours for exactly the opposite reason: at 16px, a full-depth vertex creates two needle-thin counters that fill in. **Those two constraints point in opposite directions**, so no text face will ever match — and a face that did match would be a bad text face.

Which means the goal isn't a font whose M clones the logo. Two near-identical M's sitting next to each other read as a mistake, not a system. **Match the skeleton, not the letterform.**

## The spec to shop against

Geometric sans · monolinear · circular bowls · rounded or softened terminals · low contrast.

Ranked for your case (I couldn't fetch these — the sandbox has no network — so this is category knowledge, verify by eye):

1. **Rubik** — my pick. Subtly rounded corners echo the mark's caps without going soft; a genuine workhorse UI face, variable, wide weight range.
2. **Nunito** — true rounded terminals, closest *spirit* match, still sturdy enough for interface work.
3. **Poppins / Outfit** — perfect geometric skeleton, circular, monolinear — but flat terminals, so the mark's roundness doesn't echo.
4. **Quicksand** — closest literal match (geometric + rounded), but soft enough to read twee on a power-user tool.

**Comfortaa** is the only rounded geometric you have locally, and you can see it fail in the render — too wide, too light, too idiosyncratic.

## The constraint that should actually decide this

This is a **new tab page**. It paints on every single new tab — the most frequently rendered surface in the browser. You're on `system-ui` today, which costs zero bytes, zero parse, and zero layout shift.

So I'd tier it:

- **UI text → keep `system-ui`.** Changing it buys very little and costs paint time on your hottest surface. It's already the right answer.
- **Wordmark → outline to SVG paths.** It appears in maybe three places. Outlining gives pixel-perfect fidelity, zero font loading, and sidesteps redistributing a font file inside an extension bundle. This is standard identity practice.
- **Lane titles → leave alone.** `system-ui` at 600, uppercase, `0.05em` tracking already reads as transit signage. That's why the lockups in `metro.html` work without a custom face.

## What I'd actually do

Since the wordmark gets outlined anyway, don't *pick* a font — **draw one.** Take a geometric base, redraw the M to match the mark exactly, and round the terminals across all eight letters to match the caps. Eight glyphs is an afternoon, it costs nothing at runtime, and you get coherence no off-the-shelf face will give you.

Want me to draw the outlined `Meridian` wordmark that way? I'd build it from the mark's own geometry — same 13-unit stroke, same round terminals, same square proportion — so the lockup is provably one system.

Reverted and rebuilt in the preview. Open **`img/logo-proposal/metro.html`**.

One note on the revert: your working tree has pervasive uncommitted modifications across ~120 files, so `git checkout meridian.css` would have destroyed real work. I reversed my two edits by hand instead — `meridian.css` is back to byte-identical with `meridian-extension/meridian.css`, and greps clean for `Rubik` and `--brand`.

## Rubik — bundled, not linked

Downloaded the real variable font into `img/logo-proposal/fonts/`:

- `Rubik-latin.woff2` — 35KB, **weights 300–900 in one file**
- `Rubik-latin-ext.woff2` — 19KB, only fetched if a tab title actually contains those codepoints

Verified it genuinely renders from disk: `document.fonts.check` returns true and "Meridian" measures 165.6px in Rubik vs 192.0px fallback. It's SIL OFL 1.1, so bundling and redistributing inside the extension is fine.

I used **`font-display: optional`**, not `swap`. On a surface that repaints on every new tab, `swap` means system-ui paints first and then visibly jumps to Rubik — every single time. `optional` gives a ~100ms window, keeps the fallback for that paint if the font isn't ready, and never swaps. After first load it's disk-cached, so in practice you get Rubik with zero layout shift.

**Weights drop one step.** Rubik's 600 thickens noticeably against the mark's monolinear stroke — your 600s want to be 500s, or the UI gains weight it didn't ask for. Its caps are also tight, so the signage settings carry .13–.15em tracking.

## #2ed8b0 — one measurement changes the plan

It's `hsl(166 69% 51%)` — **a light color**. That decides everything:

| | ratio | |
|---|---|---|
| on dark `#1c1c1e` | **9.37:1** | superb |
| on light `#f5f5f5` | **1.67:1** | invisible |
| white text on it | **1.82:1** | never |
| black text on it | **11.57:1** | yes |

So it can't be one token. It needs three, and the preview documents each with its measured ratio:

- **`--brand` `#2ed8b0`** — fill only. Logo disc, nameplate. Never text, never a hairline.
- **`--brand-ink` `#0d2f28`** — the only safe foreground *on* the mint (7.95:1).
- **`--brand-fg` `#15705a` light / `#2ed8b0` dark** — same hue darkened for light mode, 5.51:1. This is the brand color when it's *text or an icon*.

## The decision I need from you

**The mint breaks the toolbar icon on light.** Your M is knocked out to transparent, which means M-vs-disc contrast *is* disc-vs-background contrast. At 1.67:1 on a light toolbar the whole icon turns to fog — and 16px is where it lives.

Filling the counter with `--brand-ink` instead of leaving it transparent gives the mark internal contrast, so it holds on any surface. **Section 2 shows both, at 72/32/16, on both grounds.** The geometry is untouched — this is purely a color treatment — but it is a change to how the logo is rendered, so it's your call.

## One more thing worth deciding

Brand hue is **166**; your default `--accent-hue` is **197**. That's 31° apart — close enough to read as two slightly-different teals rather than a deliberate pair. Options are to leave it (accent is wallpaper-derived anyway, so it's rarely 197 in practice), or move the pre-JS default to 166 so the out-of-box state is coherent.

I kept `--brand` and `--accent` as separate tokens deliberately — merging them would make your logo change hue with every wallpaper.

Want me to apply the ink-counter treatment, and then port the whole token set into `meridian.css` plus the mirror?

Both clear. The first one is a real spacing bug — let me diagnose it before fixing.

Diagnosed. Two invisible culprits: 9.375% transparent padding baked into the mark's viewBox, and `letter-spacing`'s trailing space after the final N. Fixing both, plus the color and all-caps changes.

Now the lockup markup — tight viewBox, single brand color, all-caps:

Let me verify the gaps numerically rather than trust my eye.

`18.00 | 18.00 | 14.38` — but that third number is measuring the border box, which still contains the trailing tracking. Let me measure the actual ink in the rendered pixels.

My band detection caught the section label, not the lockup. Let me target the mint rails specifically.

Ground truth: **18.0 / 19.0 / 19.0 px** — was 4.7 / 20.7 / 21.9. The residual 1px is glyph sidebearing, well below perceptual threshold. Final check on the rest of the page:

Done — all three changes are in `metro.html`.

## The centering bug had two invisible causes

Neither was in the margins I'd written:

1. **The mark's viewBox carried hidden padding.** `0 0 128 128` holds a disc of `r=52` at `c=64`, so the ink spans 12–116 — **9.375% transparent padding on every side**. Flex packs boxes, not ink, so the rail butted against a box whose disc didn't start for another 4.7px. Lockups now use `viewBox="12 12 104 104"`, tight to the disc, which makes the flex `gap` the single source of spacing.
2. **`letter-spacing` appends space after the *final* letter.** MERIDIAN was carrying ~3.9px of dead air on its right that looked like a wider gap. `margin-right: -.14em` cancels exactly that.

Measured from the rendered pixels, ink-edge to ink-edge:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| rail → disc | 4.7px | **18.0px** |
| disc → MERIDIAN | 20.7px | **19.0px** |
| MERIDIAN → rail | 21.9px | **19.0px** |

The residual 1px is glyph sidebearing — below perceptual threshold, and correct to leave.

Because the tight viewBox removes the padding, I re-specified the disc sizes so they render the same visual weight: 42px station stop, 32px nameplate, 36px quiet.

## One color, both themes

`--brand-fg` is gone entirely — `#2ed8b0` at full strength everywhere, light and dark. Down to two tokens: `--brand` and `--brand-ink`. Section 1 now documents the light-mode ratio as a recorded, accepted tradeoff rather than proposing a substitute.

## Always caps

All three lockups share **one** wordmark treatment: uppercase, weight 500, `.14em` tracking, with the negative-margin correction. The quiet lockup went from 30px sentence-case to 24px caps — caps at the same size read considerably larger, so the step down keeps it the quiet one. The type-scale sample in §4 matches.

The tracking isn't optional: Rubik's caps are tight by default, and uppercase without it reads as a solid block.

One consequence of the single-color decision worth naming once: on light surfaces the mint is 1.67:1, so the knocked-out M has nothing to hold its shape at 16px. The `--brand-ink` counter treatment in §2 is now the only thing that keeps the toolbar icon legible there. That's still your call — say the word and I'll apply it, then port the tokens into `meridian.css` and the mirror.

Good — that's a counter-treatment change, not a brand-color change, so it's consistent with keeping `#2ed8b0` fixed. Implementing it as an adaptive counter.

Caught a bug — the new CSS `mask: none` also overrode section 2's hand-built demo SVGs, wiping the M from the "knockout" panel. Those need to opt out.

The scan hit the top of the disc, above the M. Let me find the disc's centerline and cross the actual stems.

My range spanned the whole lockup — the `PAGEBG` hits are the gaps between rail, disc, and text. Let me scope it to the disc alone.

Clean. Every pixel is mint, ink, or a two-color blend — one antialiasing pixel per edge, zero background bleed. Final look at all three lockups:

Ink counter is in for light mode. Open `metro.html` — §2 documents the decision, §3 shows it live.

## How it's built

The counter adapts to the ground; **the brand color never does**. `#2ed8b0` stays fixed in both themes — only the M's fill changes:

- **Dark → knockout.** A genuine hole, so a wallpaper shows through the M. Disc reads 9.37:1.
- **Light → ink counter.** `--brand-ink` at 7.95:1 against the mint, so the mark carries its own internal structure instead of depending on a 1.67:1 edge.

Geometry is byte-identical in both.

## One implementation choice worth flagging

The obvious approach — layer an ink path on top of the still-masked disc — produces a **halo**. The mask's antialiased hole edge and the path's antialiased edge each carry partial alpha, so at the boundary you get roughly 25% of the page background compositing into the M's stroke edge.

Instead I toggle the CSS `mask` property off in light mode, so the ink meets the mint directly with nothing behind it. Verified by sampling the rendered pixels straight across the disc:

```
#2ed8b0 ×10 │ #166150 │ #0d2f28 ×4 │ … │ #176251 │ #2ed8b0 ×10
```

Every pixel is mint, ink, or a two-color blend of them — exactly one transition pixel per edge, and no trace of `#f5f5f5`. Clean.

## Two things this surfaced

**The nameplate had to be excluded.** Its mark is already ink-on-mint sitting on a mint plate — applying the light-mode rule would have unmasked an ink disc *and* filled its counter with ink, collapsing it to a solid blob. It carries `.mark--plate` and keeps the knockout in both themes.

**The §2 comparison panels had to opt out.** The new CSS `mask: none` overrode their inline `mask` attributes and erased the M from the "knockout" panel — which would have made the comparison meaningless. They're now `.mark-demo`, outside the adaptive rules, so each panel hard-codes the treatment it's demonstrating.

At 16px in §2 the difference is stark: the light knockout is essentially a mint dot, the ink counter is still a legible M.

When this goes live it maps cleanly onto your existing assets — `favicon.svg` already uses a `prefers-color-scheme` block, so it's the same swap. Say the word and I'll port the tokens, the `@font-face`, and both icon sources into `meridian.css` and the mirror.

messages.content:
Nice — that's the true transit construction: the mark becomes the terminus and the line runs out to the label. There are a few ways to join them, so let me build the variants and compare.

B and D look identical — because D's overlap hides behind the disc. The real difference is at the junction. Let me magnify it.

Those non-mint columns are the ink M inside the disc, not a gap. Let me check the actual junction shoulder — where the circle curves away from the bar.

Junction is solid — B and D are pixel-identical, so D's overlap is unnecessary complexity. One more check: is the rail optically centered on the caps?

Rail sits 1px below the caps' optical center — the classic all-caps centering error, since the line box reserves descender space that caps never use. Let me get the exact em value.

Zero offset — Rubik's line-box center and cap-height center coincide exactly (both 34.5 units above baseline). My 1px pixel reading was antialiasing noise. No correction needed; good thing I checked before "fixing" it.

Finalizing on B and dropping the redundant D:

B is in — open `metro.html` §3.

## What changed

The mark is now the **terminus** at far left, with the line running out from it to the label:

**◉━━━━ MERIDIAN**

That's the actual transit construction, and it satisfies the brief in a way the old symmetric version didn't — there, the line didn't extend *from* anything, it just framed the group.

It also has a practical benefit: the lockup's left edge is now the disc itself, so it left-aligns cleanly against other content in a top bar.

## Three joins tested

- **A · detached** — line floats with gaps at both ends. Rejected: it reads as three separate objects and the line becomes a decorative dash. Nothing "extends from" the mark.
- **B · butting the disc** — **adopted.** The disc and line become one object by uniform connectedness, and that object labels the text. This is what makes it read as a stop rather than a bullet.
- **D · through-line** — rail starting at the disc's center and emerging from behind it. Dropped: it renders **pixel-identical** to B. At 3px off the centerline a `r=21` circle pulls in only **0.22px**, so a butt joint leaves no visible notch — the negative margin and `z-index` bought nothing. I left the finding in a comment in case the disc ever gets much smaller, where the math changes.

## Two details

**Squared the rail's joining end.** A rounded cap meeting a circle leaves a slivered crescent where the two curves diverge. The outer end stays rounded; only the joint is flat.

**The line stops 18px short of the text.** A bar running into caps reads as a strikethrough lead-in. The gap keeps it a route line pointing at a label.

## One thing I checked and deliberately didn't change

My pixel scan said the rail sat 1px below the caps' optical center — the classic all-caps error, since the line box reserves descender space that caps never occupy. Before correcting it I pulled Rubik's real metrics: cap ink center is 34.5 units above baseline, and the line-box center is **also** 34.5. The offset is exactly zero. That 1px was antialiasing noise between my text and solid-bar detection thresholds.

Worth flagging because it's font-specific luck, not a general rule — if the wordmark ever moves off Rubik, this needs re-measuring.

The nameplate and quiet lockups are unchanged. Ready to port the whole set into `meridian.css` and the mirror whenever you want.

  "description": "Implement the design decisions locked in `img/logo-proposal/metro.html` into the live extension. That file is the approved reference — read it first; its comments carry the reasoning behind every value below. Nothing in it has been ported yet.

**Mirror rule:** `meridian-extension/` is a runtime mirror of root. Every change must land in BOTH (`meridian.css` + `meridian-extension/meridian.css`, `components/*` + `meridian-extension/components/*`, fonts in both trees). The working tree has ~120 pre-existing uncommitted files — never `git checkout` / `git restore` anything.

**Logo geometry is unchanged.** This is type, color, and spatial treatment only.

---

### 1. Bundle Rubik locally
- Move `img/logo-proposal/fonts/Rubik-latin.woff2` and `Rubik-latin-ext.woff2` to a real runtime path (e.g. `fonts/`), in both trees.
- Copy the two `@font-face` blocks verbatim from metro.html (lines 20–40), fixing the `url()` paths. Keep `font-weight: 300 900`, `format("woff2-variations")`, both `unicode-range` declarations, and **`font-display: optional`** — `swap` would flash system-ui then jump to Rubik on every single new tab. Do not change it.
- Add `--font-ui:"Rubik",system-ui,-apple-system,sans-serif` and route `meridian.css:66`'s font stack through it.
- Rubik is SIL OFL 1.1 — ship the license file alongside the woff2s.

### 2. Weight + tracking pass
Rubik runs visually heavier than the current stack. **Drop every weight one step** (600 → 500, 500 → 400) across `meridian.css` and `components/sidebar.css`, in both trees. Any all-caps text needs **.13–.15em** tracking — Rubik's caps are tight and untracked uppercase reads as a solid block.

### 3. Brand tokens
```css
--brand:#2ed8b0;      /* FILL only — 1.67:1 on light, never text, never a hairline */
--brand-ink:#0d2f28;  /* the only legible foreground ON --brand (7.95:1) */
```
Fixed in both themes. **`--brand` and `--accent` must stay separate tokens** — `--accent` is wallpaper-derived; merging them makes the logo shift hue with the wallpaper. White on mint is 1.82:1 — never use it.

### 4. Mark: counter treatment adapts, color does not
Define the `#meridian-m` mask once (metro.html lines 174–180) in the page's SVG defs. Then:
- **Dark:** true knockout — `mask:url(#meridian-m)` on the disc, so wallpaper shows through the M (9.37:1).
- **Light:** `mask:none` + counter path stroked in `--brand-ink`. At 1.67:1 a hole has nothing to hold its shape at 16px.
- Toggle the **`mask` property**, do not layer an ink path over a still-masked disc — layering composites the page background into the M's antialiased edge at ~25% and leaves a visible halo along the stroke.
- Nameplate variant (`.mark--plate`) keeps the knockout in *both* themes; it's already ink-on-mint, so filling its counter collapses it to a blob.
- Regenerate `icon16/32/48/128.png` and `favicon.svg` from `icon-source.svg` if the ink-counter variant is needed for light-mode surfaces.

### 5. Lockups — nameplate + quiet only
Port `.lockup-plate` and `.lockup-quiet` exactly (metro.html 121–132). Two non-obvious details, both load-bearing:
- Lockup SVGs use **`viewBox="12 12 104 104"`**, not `0 0 128 128`. The disc (r=52 @ c=64) spans 12..116, so the full viewBox carries 9.375% transparent padding per side; flex sizes the box, not the ink, and that padding silently widens every gap next to the mark.
- `.wordmark` is **always caps, weight 500, .14em tracking, `margin-right:-.14em`**. letter-spacing appends space after the *final* letter too; the negative margin cancels exactly that, which matters most inside the nameplate pill where it fakes extra right padding.
- Nameplate padding is `10px 24px 10px 10px` — padding-left equals padding-top so the 32px disc sits concentric with the pill's round cap.

### 6. Lane spine
`components/WorkspaceLane.js` already emits `.workspace-lane`, `.lane-header`, `.lane-group-dot`, `.lane-title`, `.lane-tab-count`. The spine (`.lane-body::before`) does not exist yet — add the markup wrapper and the CSS from metro.html 143–156.

- `.lane-group-dot` — 13px ring: `background:var(--ground)`, `border:3.5px solid var(--group-color)`, `box-sizing:border-box`. Reconcile with the existing rule at `meridian.css:423`.
- `.lane-body` — `position:relative; padding-left:26px`.
- `.lane-body::before` — `left:3px; top:-10px; bottom:10px; width:4px; border-radius:0 0 2px 2px; background:var(--group-color); opacity:.55`, rising to `1` on `.workspace-lane:hover`, transitioned over `--transition`.
- The spine is set from each lane's Chrome tab-group color via a `--group-color` custom property on `.workspace-lane`. **Brand mint is the default only for the Ungrouped lane** — grouped lanes keep their own Chrome color.
- `left:3px` + `width:4px` centers the spine on the dot's stroke; the `top:-10px` overhang tucks it under the header so the dot reads as the spine's cap. Verify against the existing lane spacing and adjust the offsets rather than the concept if the header rhythm differs.
- `.lane-title` becomes 13px/500 uppercase at .05em; `.lane-tab-count` 11px muted at .85 opacity.

### 7. Cleanup + verification
- Remove any now-dead accent/brand duplication left behind.
- Verify in light and dark, at 16px / 32px / 72px mark sizes, with a wallpaper set and with none.
- Check the mark's edge at 16px on light specifically — that's where the halo bug would show.
- Confirm no layout shift on new-tab paint (the whole point of `font-display: optional`).
- Diff root vs `meridian-extension/` at the end to confirm the mirror is in sync.",
  "agent_id": "designer",
  "label": "Feature",
  "priority": "high",
  "status": "backlog"
}

messages.content:
Ah — the browser-level icon, not the in-page lockup. Let me look at what's actually there.

Found the real problem — and a trap. Let me confirm before writing.

A dynamic toolbar icon renderer — this is likely the actual culprit.

Now I understand the actual failure. Writing the fix.

Mark reads at every size, but I see a regression: the disc sits inside 9.4% transparent padding per side, so at 16px it renders ~13px — visibly smaller than the old full-bleed icon. Tightening the viewBox to the ink.

Full bleed now, and the M holds at 16px in every context. Mirroring.

Let me verify the recolor regex actually works against the new file — the comment worries me.

Confirmed a real bug I just introduced: the regex matched `<svg>` inside my own comment, mangled it, and left the root `fill="#1c1c1e"` untouched — the dark-toolbar icon would render near-black on dark chrome. The SVG must stay free of those tokens, so the explanation belongs in the code that imposes the constraint.

Done. The reason nothing changed was that the toolbar icon isn't the manifest PNGs at all — `utils/toolbarIcon.js` fetches `img/Meridian.svg` at runtime, recolors it, and overrides them via `chrome.action.setIcon`. That file was still the old calligraphic mark from July, so the toolbar would have kept showing the old logo no matter what the PNGs contained.

Three surfaces, three different correct treatments:

**`img/Meridian.svg`** — toolbar. Now the geometric M, monochrome, knocked out of the disc. Monochrome is deliberate here: the toolbar is chrome we don't control, at 16px, beside a dozen other extension icons, and `#2ed8b0` is 1.67:1 on a light toolbar — the mark would dissolve. The existing light/dark recolor is what keeps it legible, so I kept that mechanism and only swapped the artwork.

**`img/icon-source.svg` → `icon16/32/48/128.png`** — manifest icons, regenerated. These get an **ink counter, not a knockout**. They're composited over backgrounds we can't predict (extensions page, Web Store grid, overflow menu), and a knockout is a transparent hole that goes light-on-mint at 1.67:1 on a light backdrop. Filling the counter with `#0d2f28` puts the M at 7.95:1 against the mint, so one static artwork is safe everywhere. Worth flagging: the PNGs sitting in `img/logo-proposal/` were rendered in `#0ABAFF`, the *old* blue — copying those across would have shipped the wrong brand color.

**`img/favicon.svg`** — tab strip. The only one that can honor the counter rule directly, so it does: knockout on dark (9.37:1), ink counter on light, via `prefers-color-scheme`, with the mask *toggled* rather than an ink path layered over a masked disc.

Two things I corrected mid-way:

- **viewBox** — all three now use `12 12 104 104`, tight to the disc. At `0 0 128 128` the disc carries 9.4% transparent padding per side, so the 16px icon rendered at ~13px — noticeably smaller than the old full-bleed icon it replaces.
- **A bug I introduced.** I'd written an explanatory comment into `Meridian.svg`, and `recolorToolbarSvg`'s `/<svg\b([^>]*)>/` takes the *first* match in the document — it hit the `<svg>` inside my comment, rewrote that, and left the real root `fill="#1c1c1e"` untouched. Result: a near-black icon on dark chrome. The SVG is now comment-free and the contract is documented in `toolbarIcon.js`, where it can't break the regex. Verified both schemes resolve to exactly one root fill.

Root and `meridian-extension/` are byte-identical on all eight touched files. **You'll need to reload the unpacked extension** — Chrome caches action icons aggressively, and `chrome://extensions` → reload is usually enough; if the toolbar still looks stale, toggle the extension off and on.

Separately, still outstanding from the earlier task: the in-page lockup CSS (`.lockup-quiet`, `.wordmark`) exists in `meridian.css` but no markup uses it, so the wordmark isn't on the new tab page anywhere. That's the thing I asked about last turn — unrelated to the icon work.

messages.content:
Let me check — "correct then reverts" usually means something is overwriting it at runtime.

No app code touches the page's `<link rel="icon">`, and there are no stale copies of the old artwork left in either tree. Let me verify the SVG itself actually renders before blaming the cache.

Found it — not caching. `img/favicon.svg` is **malformed XML**:

Now confirming the favicon actually renders in real Chrome, in both schemes:

Identical file sizes — suspicious. Let me measure pixels rather than eyeball it.

Definitive: both renders are byte-identical and contain **only** mint + transparent — no `#0d2f28` ink anywhere. The media query never produced two results; the mask applied unconditionally. In an image/favicon rendering context, `prefers-color-scheme` plus CSS `mask` is not reliable — and a favicon's failure mode is silent.

Screenshot picked up page scrollbars. The SVG is static now, so a clean rasterize suffices:

No — good instinct, but it was two real bugs of mine. Caching would have been the comfortable answer; the evidence says otherwise.

**Bug 1: the file was malformed XML.** I wrote `--brand-ink` inside an XML comment, and XML forbids `--` inside comments. `xmllint` rejected it outright. That produces exactly the symptom you described: Chrome doesn't show a broken icon when a favicon fails to parse — it silently falls back to the previously cached one. Correct at first paint, then reverts to the old logo. Same defect was in `icon-source.svg`; Inkscape happened to be lenient enough to still render the PNGs, so those were fine.

**Bug 2: the adaptive treatment never worked anyway.** After fixing the XML I rendered the favicon in real Chrome under both schemes and measured the pixels instead of eyeballing them. Both renders were byte-identical and contained **only** mint and transparent — zero `#0d2f28` pixels. The `prefers-color-scheme` branch never fired and the CSS `mask` applied unconditionally. Favicons rasterize in an image context where neither is dependably honored.

So I dropped the adaptive treatment from the favicon. It's now static: mint disc, counter filled with brand ink — the same artwork as the manifest PNGs. That's 7.95:1 *inside* the mark, so the M holds on a light tab and a dark tab without the file needing to know which it is. Verified rendering at 64px and 16px on both backgrounds.

This does depart from the metro.html §2 decision that dark gets a knockout. I think that's correct here: that decision was made for the in-page mark, where the backdrop is the user's wallpaper and full CSS applies. A favicon is a different rendering context, and the deciding factor is that its failure mode is invisible — a fragile favicon that breaks looks identical to one that was never installed. The knockout still stands for the in-page mark.

The lesson generalized into the file comments: both SVGs now carry a warning to keep comments free of doubled hyphens, and `toolbarIcon.js` documents its own regex constraint from the earlier fix. All eight files validate and root/`meridian-extension/` are byte-identical.

Caching may still be layered on top of this — Chrome's favicon database is sticky and keyed by the extension URL, which doesn't change on reload. If the old icon persists after a reload now that the file is valid, a hard reload or a fresh profile will confirm which you're looking at.

messages.content:
Clear picture. Note `packagedParity.test.mjs` only diffs code files, not `img/` — which is why root has `train.webp` and the mirror has `aurora.webp` with nothing failing.

Now verifying nothing else referenced the old asset, and running the suite:

A pre-existing test covers the icon SVGs — my earlier icon work broke it and I didn't run the suite then. Let me look.

That test encodes the **old** mark (`#f5f5f7` disc behind `#1c1c1e` ink) — the design my icon work deliberately replaced. Updating it to assert the new contract, and adding a guard for the silent-failure bug I hit:

All 133 pass. Now the accent — let me find where it's defined.

Now I understand the accent architecture. Before changing anything, let me check what `train.webp` will actually derive to at runtime.

I can replicate that sampler exactly to predict the runtime accent:

Important: `train.webp`'s dominant hue is **8** (red-orange), and it clears the `s<12` gate — so the runtime sampler will actively override the accent to red-orange. A CSS default change alone won't survive. Let me compute the legible brand-hue values first.

Hard numbers now. Raw `#2ed8b0` is **1.51:1** on the light surface `#eaeaea` — and `--accent` is used as *text* color in ~8 places. That's the "FILL only, never text" rule from the spec. So brand-as-accent is only literal in dark mode; light needs the deeper solve.

Both changes are in, all 133 tests pass, mirror clean. But the accent one has a catch you need to decide on.

**Background swap — done.**
- `DEFAULT_BACKGROUND.value` → `img/train.webp`, `blur: 1`, `transparency: 0` (already 0).
- `train.webp` copied into `meridian-extension/img/`; `aurora.webp` deleted — after the swap nothing referenced it, so it was a 206 KB orphan in the package. Stale `aurora` mentions in comments and one test updated.
- Worth knowing: `packagedParity.test.mjs` only diffs code files, not `img/`. That's why root had `train.webp` and the mirror had `aurora.webp` with nothing failing. I synced them by hand.

**I broke a test earlier and hadn't noticed.** `tests/toolbarIcon.test.mjs` asserted the *old* mark (`#f5f5f7` disc, `#1c1c1e` ink group) — my icon work replaced that design, so the assertions were stale. I updated them to the new contract (mint disc, ink counter, no `mask=`) and added two regression tests for the silent failures I hit: doubled hyphens in SVG comments, and the `recolorToolbarSvg` root-fill contract. Should have run the suite during the icon work; my apologies.

**Accent — needs your call.**

I set the CSS defaults to the brand hue: `--accent-hue: 166`, `--accent-sat: 69%`, lightness 32% light / 58% dark.

Two things to know:

*It can't literally be `#2ed8b0` in light mode.* `--accent` is used as **text** color in about a dozen rules, and `#2ed8b0` on the `#eaeaea` surface is **1.51:1** — the same fill-only constraint that governs `--brand`. So light mode solves to `#198a70` (3.55:1). Dark mode at 58% gives `#4adebb` (8.27:1), which is essentially the brand color. Those numbers match what the runtime solver would pick, so there's no flash between the CSS default and the JS pass.

*The CSS default gets overridden at runtime.* I ran `train.webp` through the exact sampler in `SettingsPanel.js` — 48×48, 24-bin saturation-weighted histogram. Its dominant hue is **8** (red-orange), saturation 38, which clears the `s < 12` gate. So `applyDerivedAccent` will set `--accent-hue: 8` and you'll see a red-orange accent next to a mint logo. The CSS default only shows pre-JS or on a grayscale wallpaper.

So "brand accent by default" needs one more decision, and it's a product one I didn't want to make for you: the wallpaper-derived accent is a real feature, and pinning the accent to brand removes it. Options — pin the hue to 166 and drop derivation; keep derivation but gate it behind a setting that defaults off; or leave it as-is and accept a red-orange accent with `train.webp`. Say which and I'll wire it.

messages.content:
Let me check what you already have, since those five screenshots may or may not conform.

**1280×800.** That's the answer — and it's what your existing five already are.

The full spec:

| Asset | Size | Format |
|---|---|---|
| **Screenshots** | **1280×800** (or 640×400) | 24-bit PNG, **no alpha**, or JPEG |
| Small promo tile | 440×280 | 24-bit PNG/JPEG, no alpha |
| Marquee promo tile | 1400×560 | 24-bit PNG/JPEG, no alpha |
| Store icon | 128×128 | PNG |

Take 1280×800, not 640×400 — 640 is a legacy allowance and renders soft on the listing page. You can upload up to 5, and Google shows at least one at full width, so the first one carries the most weight. Square corners, full bleed, no letterboxing or drop shadow baked in; the store draws its own frame.

**One problem with your current set, though:** all five are **RGBA**, and the store wants 24-bit with no alpha channel. Worse, the alpha isn't even fully opaque — it ranges 241–255, so there's genuine partial transparency in there. That's probably a screenshot tool capturing the rounded/translucent window chrome. Uploads with an alpha channel get rejected or silently flattened against an unknown backdrop, which can leave a haze over the edges.

Flatten them onto an opaque background before uploading:

```
python3 -c "
from PIL import Image
import glob
for f in sorted(glob.glob('img/meridian-screen*.png')):
    im = Image.open(f).convert('RGBA')
    bg = Image.new('RGB', im.size, (28,28,30))   # or (255,255,255) for light shots
    bg.paste(im, mask=im.getchannel('A'))
    bg.save(f.replace('img/','store-assets/').replace('.png','-store.png'))
"
```

Pick the matte to match each shot's own background so the 241-alpha edge pixels blend invisibly rather than against a contrasting color.

Two other things worth flagging: your promo tile is already correct at 440×280 RGB, but it was built on the old **Ocean gradient and the old calligraphic mark** — per its README it uses `img/Meridian.svg`'s ring-and-flame strokes with a teal `hsl(197 100% 55%)` accent. That's now three brand generations behind. Same goes for the screenshots if they predate today's work — they'd show the old logo, the pre-Rubik type, and the aurora wallpaper rather than train.

If you want, I can regenerate the promo tile on the current brand and re-shoot the five screenshots against the new default wallpaper and accent once you've settled the wallpaper-derived-accent question — that decision changes what color the UI is in every screenshot, so it's worth resolving first.

Agreed — and it's more than a refresh, since `store-assets/` is currently three brand generations behind: Ocean gradient background, the old ring-and-flame mark from `Meridian.svg`, teal `hsl(197 100% 55%)` accent, and `system-ui` type instead of Rubik.

What needs regenerating:

**Promo tile (440×280)** — unblocked. It's brand art, so it should be built on `--brand` `#2ed8b0` and `--brand-ink`, not on `--accent`. New disc-and-M mark, Rubik wordmark at weight 500 / .14em tracking. The one thing to decide is the background: the Ocean gradient no longer relates to anything in the product. A deep field in the brand's own hue family, or the train wallpaper itself, would both be more honest — I'd lean train, since it's what a user actually sees on install.

**Screenshots (5 × 1280×800, flattened to RGB)** — blocked on the accent question. Whatever we decide there is the color of the UI chrome in all five shots, so re-shooting before that is wasted work.

**Marquee tile (1400×560)** — you don't have one at all. It's optional, but it's the asset Google uses if you ever get featured, and it's cheap to produce alongside the small tile.

So the accent decision is the real gate. Recap of the three options, with my recommendation:

1. **Pin accent to brand hue, drop wallpaper derivation.** Predictable, always on-brand, screenshots stay valid as you swap wallpapers. Loses a genuinely nice feature.
2. **Keep derivation, gate it behind a setting defaulting to off.** Best of both, costs a settings row and a bit of wiring.
3. **Leave as-is** — red-orange accent against a mint logo with `train.webp`. I'd avoid this one; hue 8 against hue 166 is close to complementary, and it will read as a mistake in a store screenshot.

I'd go with **2** if you want to keep the feature, **1** if you want this shipped. Either way the promo tile can start now — say the word and I'll rebuild it, and tell me whether you want train or a brand field behind it.

The `logo-proposal/` folder is gone and `metro.html` now lives at `img/metro.html` — so its `@font-face` paths are broken.

Same silent-failure class as the favicon: `../../fonts/` was correct at the old depth, but from `img/metro.html` it resolves above the project root — and `font-display: optional` means a 404 never swaps, it just quietly keeps the fallback forever.

You're right, and the cause is mechanical: `logo-proposal/` is gone and `metro.html` now sits at `img/metro.html`, but its `@font-face` still pointed at `../../fonts/`. That was correct at the old depth (`img/logo-proposal/../../fonts/` → project root); from `img/` it resolves *above* the project root. Fixed to `../fonts/`.

The reason it failed silently is `font-display: optional` — the property that stops the new-tab flash. On a 404 it never swaps, it just keeps the fallback permanently. Third silent-failure of the day, same shape as the malformed favicon and the hijacked recolor regex.

Proof it's real, not me asserting it — I rendered `metro.html` with the fixed path and again with the font forced to 404, and diffed:

Top is Rubik, bottom is what you screenshotted. Note the tighter, more geometric `M` and `R` and the narrower `D` in the fixed version; the fallback also reflows the whole page, which is why the crops sit at different offsets.

Worth knowing: the fonts load fine over `file://` — I tested with and without `--allow-file-access-from-files` and the renders were byte-identical, so you can just open `img/metro.html` directly.

For the tiles, **440×280** and **1400×560**, built on metro.html's language: `#141416` ground, the quiet lockup, Rubik 500 at .14em, mint reserved as fill with `--brand-ink` on top of it, and the existing "Spatial tab command center" tagline. Both flattened to 24-bit RGB, no alpha, full bleed.

One question before I build, because it changes the whole composition and I don't want to guess: **train wallpaper behind them, or a flat brand field?** I'd go flat `#141416` for the 440×280 — it's small, and at that size a photo becomes noise behind the lockup — and use the train photo on the 1400×560, where there's room for it to read as an image and it matches what a user sees on install. That gives you a quiet tile and a scenic marquee rather than two of the same thing.

  "content": "# Store Assets

Marketing graphics for the Chrome Web Store listing. These are **not** part of
the shipped extension package — they are uploaded in the Web Store developer
dashboard.

| Asset | Size | Source | Export |
|---|---|---|---|
| Small promotional tile | 440 × 280 | `src/promo-tile-440x280.html` | `promo-tile-440x280.png` |
| Marquee promotional tile | 1400 × 560 | `src/marquee-1400x560.html` | `marquee-1400x560.png` |

Screenshots (1280 × 800) are captured from the running extension, not generated
here.

## Design

Both tiles follow `img/metro.html`, the brand specimen. Deliberately flat brand
art — no wallpaper photo behind either one.

- **Ground** — `#1c1c1e`, the app's own dark surface token, so the tiles sit in
  the same family as the product rather than inventing a marketing palette.
- **Mark** — the disc with the M knocked out. On a dark ground the counter is a
  true hole and the mint disc reads 9.37:1. Both use `viewBox="12 12 104 104"`,
  tight to the disc: the full `0 0 128 128` frame carries 9.4% transparent
  padding per side, and since flex sizes the box rather than the ink, that
  padding would silently widen the gap next to the mark.
- **Type** — Rubik 500, always caps, `.14em` tracking, with
  `margin-right: -.14em` to cancel the space `letter-spacing` appends after the
  final letter. The wordmark is `#f5f5f7`; the tagline is `--muted` `#98989d`.
- **Color** — `#2ed8b0` as fill only, never as text or a hairline.
- **Marquee right panel** — the lane spine, abstracted to colored spines and
  blank cards with no text. It shows the product's spatial idea without being a
  simulated screenshot. Brand mint is the Ungrouped lane; grouped lanes keep
  their own Chrome tab-group color, exactly as the app behaves.

Text is minimal and factual: no rankings, awards, performance claims, browser
endorsement, or simulated UI. Full bleed, square corners, no transparent edges.

## Regenerate

Chrome headless at native resolution, then flattened to 24-bit RGB. **The store
requires no alpha channel**, and a screenshot straight out of Chrome carries
one, so the flatten step is not optional.

```bash

for spec in "promo-tile-440x280 440 280" "marquee-1400x560 1400 560"; do
```

antialiasing; without it Chrome uses subpixel rendering and the wordmark

If a wordmark renders in a generic sans, the `@font-face` path is wrong. The

messages.content:
Let me check the current state of the accent derivation code rather than answer from memory.

It's still open — and the code shows why it *looks* settled but isn't.

**What actually landed:** `meridian.css:65-67` pins the defaults to the brand hue — `--accent-hue: 166`, `--accent-sat: 69%`, lightness fallback 32% light / 58% dark. On paper an untouched install reads mint.

**What undoes it:** `applyAccentFromBackground()` is still unconditional. `meridian.js:72` calls it on every load for whatever background is active, including the shipped default. `applyDerivedAccent()` only bails when the sampled color is near-gray (`s < 12`); train.webp is well past that, so it writes inline `--accent-hue/-sat/-light` onto `:root`, and inline always beats the stylesheet. Net effect on a fresh install: mint for one frame, then a flip to train's red-orange (~hue 8). The gate was never written.

Two secondary mismatches worth knowing: derived accents use `ACCENT_SAT = 80` vs. the default's 69%, and the solver's light-mode band is 30–50% vs. the default 32% — so even a hue-166 wallpaper wouldn't land back on the declared default.

**How I'd close it.** Make wallpaper-matching an opt-in — "Match accent to wallpaper," off by default. Brand mint becomes the real default rather than a one-frame flash, and users who want their accent to track a photo get it explicitly. It also fits the existing pattern; there's already a "Fade to accent color" toggle in the same photo-adjust group. The alternative — special-casing the shipped wallpaper — means the accent changes depending on whether you *arrived at* train.webp or *picked* it, which is unexplainable in a settings panel.

One implementation constraint: gate `applyDerivedAccent()` only, never `applyOnBackground()`. The latter picks light-vs-dark lane-header text from the wallpaper's luminance — that's legibility, not branding, and must keep tracking the image regardless of the toggle.

Say the word and I'll wire the toggle.

"It" = the brand-hue pinning that fights the derivation. Let me confirm what the fallback is actually doing before I cut anything — deleting `--accent-hue` outright would invalidate the `hsl()` and blank the accent.

Tooling's there. Let me compute what train.webp actually derives to, replicating the histogram exactly (including the aspect-squashing 48×48 draw).

Confirmed, and stable across three resamplers: train.webp derives **hue 8**, solving to `#ca2e16` light (4.45:1) / `#ea553e` dark (3.89:1). Both clear the 3.5:1 target. Let me check what else reads those tokens before editing.

Mirror's in sync. One useful find in the history: the defaults were originally hue 197 to "match the default Ocean background so they agree pre-JS" — the brand-hue pinning was the later deviation. Restoring that convention.

Done. The accent is now purely wallpaper-derived, with no brand-hue pinning.

**What changed** (`meridian.css`, mirrored to `meridian-extension/`):

| token | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| `--accent-hue` | `166` (brand) | `8` (train.webp derived) |
| `--accent-sat` | `69%` | `80%` |
| `--accent-light` (light fallback) | `32%` | `44%` |

I kept the tokens rather than deleting them — `--accent` is built as `hsl(var(--accent-hue) …)`, so removing the declaration would have invalidated the whole function and left the accent unset. They're still structurally required as the fallback path.

The retune is what makes the derivation authoritative instead of merely winning a race. The defaults are now exactly what the solver produces for the shipped wallpaper, so first paint and post-analysis paint are the same color — that kills the mint→red-orange flash on every new-tab open, which was the visible symptom. `--accent-sat` was also out of step with `ACCENT_SAT = 80` in the solver; both now agree, and I noted the coupling in the comment so they don't drift again.

Verified rather than assumed: I replicated the saturation-weighted histogram against the real asset (matching the aspect-squashing 48×48 draw) across three resamplers. Hue 8 is stable in all three, solving to `#ca2e16` light at **4.45:1** and `#ea553e` dark at **3.89:1** — both clear the 3.5:1 target, so the accent stays legible as text. 133 tests pass, including `cssSeparation` and `packagedParity`; mirror is byte-identical.

**One consequence to be aware of.** Those defaults are also the fallback when a background has *no* derivable hue — grayscale photos, "none", near-neutral solids — because `applyDerivedAccent()` clears the inline vars in that case. Those backgrounds now get red-orange where they previously got mint. `--brand` is untouched at `#2ed8b0`, so on a grayscale wallpaper you'd see a mint logo against a red-orange accent. That's the honest consequence of "always derive" — there's nothing to derive from, so it falls back to the shipped default's color. If you'd rather the *no-hue* case return to mint, that's a one-line split (separate fallback hue from the pre-analysis default) and it doesn't reintroduce the flash.

from PIL import Image
import math, sys

def rgb_to_hsl(r,g,b):
    r/=255; g/=255; b/=255
    mx=max(r,g,b); mn=min(r,g,b)
    l=(mx+mn)/2; d=mx-mn; h=0.0; s=0.0
    if d!=0:
        s=d/(1-abs(2*l-1))
        if mx==r: h=((g-b)/d)%6
        elif mx==g: h=(b-r)/d+2
        else: h=(r-g)/d+4
        h=round(h*60)
        if h<0: h+=360
    return h, round(s*100), round(l*100)

def rel_lum(r,g,b):
    a=[]
    for v in (r,g,b):
        n=v/255
        a.append(n/12.92 if n<=0.03928 else ((n+0.055)/1.055)**2.4)
    return 0.2126*a[0]+0.7152*a[1]+0.0722*a[2]

def analyze(path, resample):
    im=Image.open(path).convert("RGBA").resize((48,48), resample)
    BINS=24
    weight=[0.0]*BINS; sSum=[0]*BINS; lSum=[0]*BINS; count=[0]*BINS
    lumSum=0.0; lumN=0
    for (r,g,b,al) in im.getdata():
        if al<125: continue
        lumSum+=rel_lum(r,g,b); lumN+=1
        h,s,l=rgb_to_hsl(r,g,b)
        if s<18 or l<10 or l>92: continue
        bin=int((h/360)*BINS)%BINS
        weight[bin]+=s/100; sSum[bin]+=s; lSum[bin]+=l; count[bin]+=1
    lum=lumSum/lumN if lumN else None
    top=-1; topW=0.0
    for b_ in range(BINS):
        if weight[b_]>topW: topW=weight[b_]; top=b_
    if top<0: return None, lum, weight
    dom={"h":round(((top+0.5)/BINS)*360),"s":round(sSum[top]/count[top]),"l":round(lSum[top]/count[top])}
    return dom, lum, weight

def hsl_to_rgb(h,s,l):
    s/=100; l/=100
    c=(1-abs(2*l-1))*s
    x=c*(1-abs(((h/60)%2)-1))
    m=l-c/2
    if h<60: r,g,b=c,x,0
    elif h<120: r,g,b=x,c,0
    elif h<180: r,g,b=0,c,x
    elif h<240: r,g,b=0,x,c
    elif h<300: r,g,b=x,0,c
    else: r,g,b=c,0,x
    return ((r+m)*255,(g+m)*255,(b+m)*255)

def contrast(l1,l2):
    hi=max(l1,l2); lo=min(l1,l2)
    return (hi+0.05)/(lo+0.05)

ACCENT_SAT=80
def solve(hue, dark, surf_hex):
    surf=rel_lum(*[int(surf_hex[i:i+2],16) for i in (1,3,5)])
    target=3.5
    floor=48 if dark else 30
    ceil=70 if dark else 50
    l=58 if dark else 44
    step=2 if dark else -2
    for _ in range(40):
        r,g,b=hsl_to_rgb(hue,ACCENT_SAT,l)
        if contrast(rel_lum(r,g,b),surf)>=target: break
        l+=step
        if l<=floor: l=floor; break
        if l>=ceil: l=ceil; break
    r,g,b=hsl_to_rgb(hue,ACCENT_SAT,l)
    return l, "#%02x%02x%02x"%(round(r),round(g),round(b)), contrast(rel_lum(r,g,b),surf)

for name,resample in (("BILINEAR",Image.BILINEAR),("LANCZOS",Image.LANCZOS),("BOX",Image.BOX)):

messages.content:
Only hit is a docs manifest. Let me rule out dynamic construction (e.g. `img/${browser}.svg`) and check whether the packaging tests enumerate them.

**Yes, they can be cleaned.** `chrome.svg` and `edge.svg` have zero references in any JS, CSS, HTML, or `manifest.json`.

I checked for dynamic construction too, since a `img/${browser}.svg` lookup wouldn't show up in a literal grep — the only templated `img/` path in the repo is in `toolbarIcon.test.mjs`, and it iterates a fixed list of three (`favicon.svg`, `icon-source.svg`, `Meridian.svg`). The `chrome` hit in `manifest.json` is `chrome_url_overrides`, unrelated. Their sole mention is `docs/release-validation.md:110,112`, which is a packaged-file manifest, not a consumer.

**That manifest is itself stale**, which weakens it as evidence of anything: it lists `img/aurora.webp`, and that file no longer exists in either tree after the train.webp swap. It needs a refresh regardless of what you decide here.

While confirming, I found the same question has a much more expensive answer next door:

| asset | code refs | size |
|---|---|---|
| `chrome.svg` + `edge.svg` | 0 | 9 KB |
| `emberstone.png` | 0 (`.svg` is the one used, 3 refs) | 13 KB |
| `Meridian.ai` | 0 | 610 KB |
| `meridian-screen1-4.png` | 0 | ~4.8 MB |

`meridian-extension/img/` is **5.5 MB, of which ~5.4 MB is unreferenced** — an Illustrator source file and four Chrome Web Store screenshots are being packaged into the shipped CRX. Users download all of it. The store screenshots are uploaded through the Developer Dashboard, not served from the extension, so they have no reason to be in the package at all; `Meridian.ai` is a design source that belongs in the repo but not in the build.

Worth separating the two decisions, though. The screenshots and `.ai` should leave `meridian-extension/` but probably stay in the root tree — that's your only copy of the logo source. `chrome.svg`/`edge.svg`/`emberstone.png` look deletable outright from both.

Want me to do the removals? I'd suggest dropping the four confirmed-dead files from both trees, pruning the ~5.4 MB from the extension mirror only, and refreshing the `release-validation.md` manifest to match reality in the same pass — then re-running the suite so `packagedParity` confirms the mirror is still coherent.

messages.content:
Let me see exactly what's diverged before copying anything — the mirror isn't a straight copy of root (it excludes `tests/`, `docs/`, `metro.html`, and carries its own extras).

Two things to sort out before I sync — you also replaced `train.webp`, and the accent defaults I pinned are derived from that exact file.

Good thing I checked. Two issues, one of which you'll want to weigh in on.

Synced and green. Let me verify one thing I noticed in the histogram — the new image's hue is unstable, and I think I see why.

Understood — stopping the accent analysis there. Runtime derivation is untouched and stays the authority.

One loose end though: the comment I wrote last turn makes a specific factual claim tied to the *old* train.webp ("these are what img/train.webp resolves to, so first paint matches"). You've since swapped that image, so that sentence is now false. Let me correct the comment without re-tuning anything.

**Synced.** Every file in `meridian-extension/` now matches its root counterpart byte-for-byte, 133 tests pass.

What I carried across, since your root edits were more than the CSS:

- **Deleted from the mirror** to match your root deletions: `chrome.svg`, `edge.svg`, `emberstone.png`, `Meridian.ai`, and `meridian-screen1-4.png`. All eight are in git HEAD, so they're recoverable if you want the `.ai` source back in the repo.
- **Copied `train.webp`** — you'd swapped the actual image, not just recompressed it (1672×941 → 1586×992), so the mirror was serving a different wallpaper than root.
- **Copied `meridian.css`** with the comment correction.

`meridian-extension/img/` went from **5.5 MB to 172 KB**. That's the packaged extension size, so it's a real download win for users.

`img/metro.html` stayed root-only — it's your untracked sandbox and doesn't belong in the package.

On the accent: I left the runtime derivation exactly as it was, and I left the fallback values alone. I only rewrote the comment, which had claimed those numbers were matched to `img/train.webp` for a flash-free first paint — true of the old image, not the new one. It now describes them as what they are: a static fallback for the pre-analysis frame and for backgrounds with no derivable hue, chosen for contrast (4.45:1 light, 3.89:1 dark) rather than to match any wallpaper.

One thing worth knowing but not acting on: the new train.webp is much less saturated than the old one, so its hue signal is weak enough that the dominant bin isn't stable — it lands on red-orange or amber depending on the downscaling filter. Your call whether that ever matters; the derived accent stays legible either way.

Default accent is now the brand mint. Mirrored, parity clean, 133 pass.

|---|---|---|
| dark | `#2cd8b0` — brand exactly | 7.69:1 |

Light mode is the one place I couldn't use `#2ed8b0` literally. `--accent` is used as **text** in about a dozen places, and `#2ed8b0` measures **1.51:1** on the `#eaeaea` surface — effectively invisible. So light mode keeps the brand hue (166) and saturation (69%) and only drops lightness until it's legible. Dark mode carries the brand color exactly. It's the same reason `--brand` is documented fill-only.

I kept it as hue/sat/lightness rather than a hex because the runtime solver overrides those channels individually — a flat hex couldn't be partially overridden, and you asked me to leave derivation alone.

**Worth being clear about what you'll actually see**, since it's the thing that started this thread: this is the *default*, and derivation still overrides it. On the shipped train.webp wallpaper the solver will find that image's hue and override to it, so mint shows on backgrounds with no derivable hue (grayscale, "none", near-neutral solids) and as the pre-analysis frame — not on the default wallpaper. If you want mint to survive on train.webp too, that needs the derivation gated, which you'd told me to leave alone. Say the word and it's a small change.

Yes — it's written. `docs/store-listing.md` §1 "Detailed description" (lines 31–59) is the Overview field. Let me check it still matches the code, since it's dated July 26 and a lot has moved since.

Yes — it's written and it's thorough. **`docs/store-listing.md` §1, lines 31–59** is the Overview field (the dashboard calls it "Detailed description"). The file also covers the Summary, single-purpose statement, all data-type declarations, and paste-ready justifications for every permission.

I spot-checked it against the code rather than just pointing at it. What holds:

- **Summary is 109 chars**, inside the 132 limit.
- **Picsum claim is accurate** — `SettingsPanel.js:1021` still fetches `picsum.photos` seeds, so the external-requests disclosure is still true. That's the one I most wanted to confirm, since a stale privacy claim is the kind that gets a submission rejected.

What's drifted, though — the doc is dated **July 26**, and its §6 reconciliation notes certify accuracy *as of that date*:

**Two shipped features are missing from the Overview.** The feature list never mentions the **side panel** or the **bookmarks button/panel**. The side panel is the bigger problem: `manifest.json` declares both the `sidePanel` permission and a `side_panel` entry, and there's a full `sidebar.{js,html,css}` implementation. A reviewer comparing the manifest to the listing sees a permission with no corresponding described feature — exactly the mismatch that draws a single-purpose query. The permission justification in §4 describes it, but the user-facing Overview doesn't.

**Today's changes aren't reflected either** — bundled Rubik (which also means a new `fonts/Rubik-OFL.txt` license obligation), the bundled default wallpaper, and the brand accent work. None of that changes a privacy claim, but §6 asserts a verification date that no longer matches the tree.

Worth noting the Overview copy itself is well-built — factual, no rankings or performance claims, no simulated-UI language, consistent terminology with the privacy policy. It just needs the two features added and a re-verification pass.

Want me to draft the revised Overview with the side panel and bookmarks panel worked into the feature list, and refresh the §6 reconciliation notes? I'd keep the existing voice and structure — this is an update, not a rewrite.

=== store-assets/README.md ===
# Store Assets

Marketing graphics for the Chrome Web Store listing. These are **not** part of
the shipped extension package — they are uploaded in the Web Store developer
dashboard.

| Asset | Size | Source | Export |
|---|---|---|---|
| Small promotional tile | 440 × 280 | `src/promo-tile-440x280.html` | `promo-tile-440x280.png` |
| Marquee promotional tile | 1400 × 560 | `src/marquee-1400x560.html` | `marquee-1400x560.png` |

Screenshots (1280 × 800) are captured from the running extension, not generated
here.

## Design

Both tiles follow `img/metro.html`, the brand specimen. Deliberately flat brand
art — no wallpaper photo behind either one.

- **Ground** — `#1c1c1e`, the app's own dark surface token, so the tiles sit in
  the same family as the product rather than inventing a marketing palette.
- **Mark** — the disc with the M knocked out. On a dark ground the counter is a
  true hole and the mint disc reads 9.37:1. Both use `viewBox="12 12 104 104"`,
  tight to the disc: the full `0 0 128 128` frame carries 9.4% transparent
  padding per side, and since flex sizes the box rather than the ink, that
  padding would silently widen the gap next to the mark.
- **Type** — Rubik 500, always caps, `.14em` tracking, with
  `margin-right: -.14em` to cancel the space `letter-spacing` appends after the
  final letter. The wordmark is `#f5f5f7`; the tagline is `--muted` `#98989d`.
- **Color** — `#2ed8b0` as fill only, never as text or a hairline.
- **Marquee right panel** — the lane spine, abstracted to colored spines and
  blank cards with no text. It shows the product's spatial idea without being a
  simulated screenshot. Brand mint is the Ungrouped lane; grouped lanes keep
  their own Chrome tab-group color, exactly as the app behaves.

Text is minimal and factual: no rankings, awards, performance claims, browser
endorsement, or simulated UI. Full bleed, square corners, no transparent edges.

## Regenerate

Chrome headless at native resolution, then flattened to 24-bit RGB. **The store
requires no alpha channel**, and a screenshot straight out of Chrome carries
one, so the flatten step is not optional.

```bash
cd store-assets/src

for spec in "promo-tile-440x280 440 280" "marquee-1400x560 1400 560"; do
  set -- $spec
  google-chrome --headless --disable-gpu --disable-lcd-text --hide-scrollbars \
    --force-device-scale-factor=1 --virtual-time-budget=6000 \
    --default-background-color=1c1c1eff --window-size=$2,$3 \
    --screenshot=/tmp/$1.png "file://$PWD/$1.html"
done

python3 -c "
from PIL import Image
for name in ('promo-tile-440x280','marquee-1400x560'):
    im = Image.open(f'/tmp/{name}.png').convert('RGBA')
    bg = Image.new('RGB', im.size, (28,28,30))
    bg.paste(im, mask=im.getchannel('A'))
    bg.save(f'../{name}.png')
"
```

Two flags are load-bearing. `--disable-lcd-text` forces grayscale
antialiasing; without it Chrome uses subpixel rendering and the wordmark
exports with red/blue color fringing on every stem. `--virtual-time-budget`
gives the webfont time to load — the sources use `font-display: block` so a
slow font can never export as a fallback sans.

If a wordmark renders in a generic sans, the `@font-face` path is wrong. The
sources reach the repo root with `../../fonts/`, and a miss is silent: the
fallback is simply kept, with no console error and no visual warning.
